opus-5.5.text:
I think the deepest reason is that the things that make a system good at the physical world and the things that make it good at knowledge work aren't actually as separate as they look. When you watch a person fold laundry or cook a meal, there's a huge amount of understanding happening: what objects are, what they're for, what the person in the kitchen wants, what happens if you push on this or pour that. That's the same kind of common sense a model needs to be a good assistant or a good researcher. It's just expressed through a body instead of through text.

And if you build separate systems, you lose the chance for each to strengthen the other. Language models have absorbed an enormous amount of semantic knowledge from the internet, and we've seen in robotics that plugging that knowledge in gives you generalization you'd never get from robot data alone. A robot can follow an instruction about an object it's never seen because the model already knows what that object is. Going the other way, I suspect physical experience gives you a grounding that text alone doesn't provide: causality, consequences, what it actually means to make a plan and have it fail. That's valuable for reasoning in general, not just for moving arms around.

There's also a practical scaling argument. The history of machine learning over the last decade is basically that general models trained on lots of diverse data beat specialized ones. If that holds, the most capable robot is going to be the one built on top of the most capable general model, and you'd want robotics to be one more modality that this model handles rather than a separate track that has to reinvent everything.

And honestly, I think it's where the biggest impact is. Knowledge work is important, but a huge fraction of what people actually spend their time on, and what the economy actually runs on, is physical. A system that can reason about a problem and then go do something about it in the real world is a much bigger deal than either half on its own.

r001.rationale: The response says physical experience provides grounding, causality, and consequences, but does not state that pursuing a task helps the model identify which parts of its observations are relevant.

r002.rationale: It says physical experience provides grounding that text alone lacks and that this grounding is valuable for reasoning in general, conveying that physical understanding can aid abstract reasoning.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that I don't think of them as two different problems. The thing that makes a model useful for knowledge work is that it has a broad understanding of the world, of what people want, of how tasks decompose, of what counts as done. A robot needs exactly that same understanding, it just has to express it through a body instead of through a text box. If you had a separate model for robotics that only knew about motor commands and camera images, it would be missing most of what makes a task make sense. Why is the kitchen organized this way, what does "clean up" mean in this particular house, what should you do when something unexpected happens. Those are not robotics questions, those are just understanding-the-world questions.

The other reason is more practical. Robotics has always been data starved. We can't scrape the internet for a billion hours of robot experience. But we can scrape the internet for a tremendous amount of knowledge about how the physical world works, what objects are, how people use tools, and if the same model that absorbs all of that can also be grounded in robot experience, then the robot gets to inherit all of that for free. The physical experience teaches the model how to actually act, and the rest of the model's knowledge tells it what to do and why. Splitting those apart throws away the main thing that's going to make robots work.

And I'd go a bit further. I actually think the robotics side will make the knowledge work side better too. A lot of what's brittle about current language models is that they've never had to deal with consequences. They say something, and it's just text. When a model has to pour a cup of coffee and it gets it wrong, coffee ends up on the floor, and that's a very different kind of feedback. Learning from real interaction with the world is how you get models that have a genuine sense of cause and effect rather than just a statistical sense of what tends to follow what. So I think the convergence is not just convenient, it's where the most capable systems are going to come from.

r001.rationale: The response says models need broad world understanding and task knowledge, but does not state that pursuing a task helps determine which parts of its observations are relevant.

r002.rationale: It says real-world interaction and physical consequences can give models a genuine sense of cause and effect, improving their knowledge-work abilities beyond text-based learning.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think the biggest reason is that these capabilities should reinforce each other. If you’re a robot trying to do something in the physical world, you don’t want to have to learn everything through physical interaction. If someone asks you to make dinner, knowing about recipes, ingredients, and people’s preferences is useful. A lot of that knowledge is already available in language, and you’d like the robot to be able to draw on it.

But I also think there’s something valuable in the other direction. Acting in the world gives you a way to test your understanding. You can have an explanation for how something works, but when you actually try to use it, you find out whether that explanation makes the right predictions. Robotics provides that kind of feedback in a very direct way.

So the hope is that we don’t end up with one system that knows things and another system that does things, with a narrow interface between them. We’d like knowledge to inform action, and experience to improve knowledge. That doesn’t necessarily mean every part of the system has to be identical, but there’s a strong reason to want those capabilities to share a common foundation.

r002.rationale: It says language knowledge can inform physical action and physical experience can test explanations, but does not say understanding the physical world beyond language helps solve abstract problems.

sol-6.1.text:
Because I think those capabilities are complementary. If you have a robot that can move things around but doesn’t understand much about the world, it’s going to be very limited. You’d like it to understand your intentions, reason about what needs to happen, and draw on the same knowledge that makes a language model useful when you’re sitting at a computer.

And the transfer could go the other way, too. Interacting with the physical world gives you a way to learn things that are hard to learn just by reading. You take an action, something happens, and you find out whether your understanding was right. My hope is that learning from that interaction can improve the model’s reasoning more broadly.

That doesn’t mean every task needs the same hardware or exactly the same training procedure. But having a shared model means that what it learns in one setting can potentially help it in another. You don’t want your robot to have to rediscover everything that your language model already knows.
